status_summary: Parts of the narrowing are operative and parts are only proposed. CISA lost about a third of its workforce after January 2025, election-security and foreign-influence/disinformation staff were reported placed on administrative leave in February 2025, and DHS ended all advisory committee memberships on 2025-01-20 (sources reviewed name the Cyber Safety Review Board but not the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee). The FY2027 budget request of 2026-04-07 would, per press reports, cut about $707 million, end programs aimed at countering misinformation, dissolve the stakeholder-engagement and international offices and, per one outlet, eliminate the election security program; Congress has not enacted it. A CRS analysis of 2026-06-09 states the request as $2.49 billion for CISA, $109 million above the FY2026 request and $386 million (13.4 percent) below the FY2025 continuing-resolution level, a different baseline from the press reports' $707 million figure, and the part of the CRS text read does not address election security or counter-misinformation. No proposal to move CISA to Transportation, or emergency communications and chemical facility roles to FEMA, was found, and in June 2026 DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin described plans for structural change while seeking to hire up to 600 more staff. On 2026-09-24 CISA released a 2026 election infrastructure security plan that relies on regional directors and threat-sharing tools and does not restore dedicated election adviser positions, while the budget request would still eliminate the election security program, per Nextgov.

timeline.event: Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman issues a memo ending all memberships on DHS advisory committees, effective immediately; reports name the Cyber Safety Review Board and do not name the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee.

A letter from Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs to the state's congressional delegation reports that CISA employees in its Election Security and Resilience Division and its Foreign Influence Operations and Disinformation initiative were placed on administrative leave, and describes uncertainty over federal funding for the election-focused information sharing center (EI-ISAC).

Cybersecurity Dive reports CISA has lost about a third of its workforce since January 2025 and is preparing a Cybersecurity Division reorganization that will turn off some programs and prioritize operational technology security, cyber intelligence and collaborative defense.
DHS funding lapse begins; congressional testimony cited by CRS says CISA furloughed roughly 60 percent of staff. P.L. 119-86, enacted 2026-04-30, ended the lapse for most of DHS including CISA.

The FY2027 budget request proposes cutting about $707 million from CISA (to roughly $2 billion), dissolving the stakeholder-engagement and international affairs offices, terminating programs focused on countering misinformation and propaganda, and removing school safety initiatives; a separate outlet reports it would also eliminate the election security program and shift some infrastructure security and emergency communications responsibilities to state and local governments. SecurityWeek reports Congress had cut the proposed FY2026 reduction from $491 million to about $135 million.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin tells the House Homeland Security Committee CISA will undergo significant structural changes, that a Senate-confirmed director will be nominated (Nick Andersen is acting director), and that the FY2027 budget proposes cutting more than $700 million; the report does not mention relocating CISA or moving its functions to other agencies.

A CRS analysis of the FY2027 DHS request states that CISA's request is 2.49 billion dollars, 109 million above the FY2026 request and 386 million (13.4 percent) below the FY2025 continuing-resolution level, with a research and development account of 44 million dollars partly from moving Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction work to CISA; the text read does not cover election security, counter-misinformation or program eliminations, and says CISA's staffing fell sharply in the six months to March 2026.

OMB Director Russell Vought tells lawmakers he will work with Secretary Mullin on rehiring for CISA, which Mullin has said he wants to expand by 600 staff; acting director Andersen says CISA expects nearly 200 job offers by the end of June.

DHS publishes a Federal Register notice (91 FR 40022) establishing ANCHOR-CI, an advisory body of sector and cross-sector councils that advises the Secretary through the CISA Director; the notice does not mention the Cybersecurity Advisory Committee.

CISA releases its 2026 Election Infrastructure Security Plan (regional directors as election security advisers, threat-sharing platform); Nextgov notes it does not restore dedicated election adviser positions and that the FY2027 request would eliminate the election security program.

title: Narrow CISA to two core missions and end its counter-disinformation work
uncertainties: Not verified: whether the CISA Cybersecurity Advisory Committee specifically was terminated (reports of the 2025-01-20 DHS memo name only the Cyber Safety Review Board; a Federal Register search for the committee returned no termination or meeting notice); the date and form of the end of CISA's mis/disinformation work (evidence is staff leave reported in a state official's letter, plus the FY2027 proposal to terminate such programs); and the FY2027 election-security elimination, which rests on one trade outlet. The 2026 staffing figures differ across outlets (about 1,000 positions lost; a target of 2,800 staff reported against about 2,200 currently, which the source itself left unclear). An AOL copy of a report on 12 CISA employees placed on leave returned an error and was not used. Searches run: CSAC termination, CISA election and disinformation staff, CISA director and FY2027 budget; no search found any proposal to move CISA to Transportation. The DHS FY2027 CISA budget document and DHS Budget in Brief (found through search; dates taken from file names) returned HTTP 403 for the CISA document and were not opened, so the program eliminations rest on SecurityWeek, The Next Web and Nextgov. CRS R48979 (read through its first 100,000 characters) gives CISA's FY2027 request as 2.49 billion dollars against the FY2026 request and the FY2025 continuing resolution, which does not reconcile with the press reports of a 707 million dollar cut to about 2 billion dollars; the comparison base for the 707 million figure was not established, so the size of the proposed cut is uncertain.
